title: How does one get into silent films?

commenti.body:
I would say just watch what you like. If you’ve given a bunch of the well known films a chance and only one landed for you, maybe they’re just not for you. And that’s okay! Watching movies shouldn’t be homework. It shouldn’t be a struggle. Watch what you like.

I could say things like give The General or Safety Last a shot, but I imagine you either have or they’re on your list anyway. So I don’t know. 

Personally, there are a number of silents I’ve enjoyed but it’s a well I go back to sparingly.

What makes you interested in watching them? 

For me it was non-silent movies that made me interested in silent films. Singing in the Rain, Jackie Chan films, The Fall. Or modern takes like The Artist. 

My favorite silent films are The Man with a Movie Camera, All Quiet on a Western Front, and The General. I recently watched The Passion of Joan of Arc and Maria Falconetti was captivating. 

Early cinema is like a Time Machine, but I think it helps to read essays or watch video essays to provide more context around the time period or creators. It’s interesting to see how they inspired future creators or invented techniques we take for granted today.

Metropolis is a cold and stylistic film. I would look to Chaplin or Keaton for more human warmth. Also Diary of a Lost Girl for a bit of pre code German decadence.

I find watching a silent movie on a big screen, with an audience and live music is different than just watching a Blu-ray or whatever. Seeing The Passion of Joan of Arc accompanied by a group of musicians is one of my favourite moviegoing experiences.

As to the easiest way to get into silent film, I'd say watching one of the best shorts from Keaton or Chaplin, like One Week or The Immigrant. I think in his 1930s movies, City Lights and Modern Times, Chaplin is drawing a lot on the shorts he made 20 years earlier, returning to similar gags and ideas.

If City Lights didn't get you I'm not sure the silent portion of the medium ever will. Not because I think everyone *has* to like it or anything, but moreso because it's probably even more accessible the Modern Times, The Navigator or The General. The storyline is rather contemporary, the performances range from subtle to downright heart-wrenching and it has sound effects and a score to boot. Like I'm not gonna come in here and tell you to watch Terje Vigen as if it's going to change your mind when, accessible as I may find it, you don't see Chaplin as a decent entry point to begin with

I don't think there's any proper way to enjoy them. They're cinema just like The Avengers or Casino or Breathless is cinema. If you want to come in with an ironic eye where you appreciate the technical aspects and throw aside the storytelling, that's valid in some form. But there's not a technique for those of us who enjoy silent films. For reference, some of my favorite silent flicks include:

Terje Vigen (1917)

Underworld (1927)

Bed and Sofa (1927)

City Lights (1931)

The Fall of the House of Usher (1928)

I Was Born, but... (1932)

The Great White Silence (1920)

Just wanted to echo The Passion of Joan of Arc! I grew up struggling to really appreciate silent films, and this one really kicked things off for me due to its advanced stylistic choices and deeply compelling performance by Renée Falconetti.

I think with any generation of movies, you have to learn and expect the different intricacies. Technology, style, message, humour, fashion, society struggles, limitations etc. they all change over time. It does take a change of mindset.

The same as you. Singin in the Rain, Sunset Boulevard etc. Films that weren't so far removed from the silent era and explored what it was like for it to just be recent history. I think it's a very interesting era in film history but it hasn't quite translated to enjoyment for me
The Passion of Joan of Arc is an incredible one. I may go with the shorts though, thank you
Thank you!

It's hard to top Metropolis.  You might try other German expressionist films like Cabinet of Dr. Caligari and Nosferatu.  

You could also try watching some Soviet montage, since it's pretty influential on modern filmmaking, Battleship Potemkin is my favorite of these.  

For me, I just have to make sure that the only thing I'm doing is watching a silent film, since I tend to be a constant multitasker.  That helps me absorb the mood and atmosphere more.
I highly recommend Buster Keaton shorts. Do yourself a favor and binge those for a while, the man was brilliant and hilarious

I like silent movies a lot. But I don’t like the comedies. I think humor changes a lot culturally. And, if it’s based on then current politics, it’s not going to hold up. Some of the attempted epics are overwrought and ridiculous. I tend to avoid those. De Mille is one I avoid, whether silent or sound. 

One of the things I like about silent films is that they’re pre-Code. There’s often an honesty to them that was quashed under the Code. 

Especially in the early days of film, there were a lot of women writing and directing, so the female characters aren’t set dressing. There were also a lot of films made by Black writers and directors. Women and BIPOC writers and directors disappeared under the studio system. 

I miss TMC’s silent Sundays. They had a lot of good movies.

I love silent films but I still struggle with them and I've been watching them for almost twenty years now. I mean, they are hard to get into for me. Like you, I find my mind wandering during the course of a silent film more so than any other genre or time period of film.

My best advice is to watch Metropolis again, and then maybe a third time. Metropolis was my first silent film, too, and I absolutely loved it. 

I think you might like any silent film if you re-watch it but you do have to monitor that; if you feel it isn't worth it then listen to your gut. But I guess what I am saying is if you don't feel like you didn't take everything in on the first viewing then try it a second time, and a third time if you still feel like you didn't fully pay attention to every scene because watching silent film is a bit of a workout: you really do have to concentrate hard in the first moments of a silent film or else the concentration takes a permanent break for the rest of the film. And I can tell you I never concentrate that well on any silent film the first time I view it. But a second and third time helps me tune in more because the first viewing warmed me up to fully concentrating another time around.

The thing to know about silent film and which is key to know and is something I actually learned from Roger Ebert is that silent films are displays of exaggerated emotions with very simple stories. I mean look at the inter titles: they're not exactly Shakespeare. So silent film stories aren't complicated (maybe except for Fritz Lang's Spies which has a convoluted plot), and they are really more about heightened drama with bold and colorful facial movements, and body gestures. You are basically watching opera without the music. 

Speaking of music, almost every silent film I've seen has had a great orchestral soundtrack playing in the background. This might be due to whoever released it as there are different companies that release the films but if nothing else, enjoy the music!  The Crowd(1928), Sunrise (1927), Pandora's Box (1928), The Man Who Laughs(1928), all had great music to go along with it but again, depends on the edition you watch. Basically, think Disney's Fantasia from 1940, 41'...you watch that differently than you watch regular movies with dialogue and sound. I know it is now quite the same thing but still it cuts along the same path.

Also, don't watch a silent film expecting great displays of artistic camera angles and such. If you understand German Expressionism, and I'm not an expert but if you know the use of shadows and angles that are expressed in a film like Metropolis or Dr Caligari, you can appreciate it more. But don't expect there to be a constant influx of that expressionistic flair in every scene or else you'll be disappointed. There are lots of boring scenes without a hint of the director's intentional interpretation of the scenery through use of the camera so don't be terribly disappointed. Make it a game, almost: spot the times where a camera shot signnifies a very important moment and then notice how it makes you feel and if you don't feel anything, fine, no big deal, doesn't mean you're not bright, it just didn't hit you. But you might see what the director was trying to do in capturing a feeling. 

If you watch Sunrise and see the lady from the city seduce the main character out of his little homestead in the country, you will see the camera move along a muddy trail of footsteps, and this is one thing you can note. Another thing is how the camera contrasts her cradling the man in her arms with the man's wife back at home and notice how strange and eerie that is. You might be intrigued or not but at least you can see how delicate the camera works its way from one idea to another. If you understand that the director, FW Murnau was an innovator in fluid camera movement then you might appreciate his work even more.

Can’t believe no one’s mentioned Laurel and Hardy. Check out Liberty, where they accidentally end up on a skyscraper construction site. For a non-comedy, check out The Cabinet of Dr Caligari, they have it on Amazon prime at the moment with an added soundtrack and voice dialog, it’s the first horror movie and did indeed give me the chills

I think one thing that don't get talked about often is the music. Silent films are of course very seldom actually silent, they almost always have a score, either the one intended from the start, or something that later restorationists have decided fits. A lot of silent movies have been ruined by boring or inappropriate soundtrack. When you choose a silent movie, check out what versions there are available, both how well-restored they are and what kind of soundtracks you might be able to find.  

For example, for a handful of the most classic Swedish silent movies, there are great newly-composed soundtracks by Matti Bye. I don't think I'd've appreciated *The Phantom Carriage*, as great as it is, as much if I hadn't seen it with a score as great as his.  

Or you can of course make your own soundtrack, put on an album or playlist you think will fit the movie (obviously hard before you've seen it).

If they're not your thing that's ok, though it sounds like you've only had limited exposure and as with modern films there's quite a broad spectrum out there. The more you watch the more you may come to appreciate what they're doing as well.

Based on what you've said my three main recommendations would be-

Sherlock Jr, to my mind possibly Keatons best and relatively short. Once the story gets going it moves at a hundred miles an hour and doesn't stop, far more propulsive than equally great fearure lengths like the general. What Keaton is  doing physically with the stunts is mind blowing and  hard to believe as well and up there with any modern counterparts like Jackie chan.

Man With A Movie Camera, narrative free and no inter titles and often classed as a "documentary" but personally I don't feel it is as its creating its own reality. There is an absolutely banging incredible modern score that coupled with the visuals make this actually quite thrilling. Seeing the filmmaker soaring and creating a new visual world using cinema as it never had been before is awesome too.

Nosferatu, such a familiar and awesome story that you (may) already know and love but told in such an incredible visually striking way, easy to get absorbed in cause you know the story so can j8st wallow in the visual choices in telling it this way.

Not sure if that helps, all greats but not a list of the top 3 and could mention a load more but each of those 3 offer different ways to possibly connect with silent movies others can't.

There are silent films which are more easy to modern audiences, like Buster Keaton's ones for instance, or the very early movies (Lumière, Meliès, Brighton...) which are more conceptual with their one-minute-duration, and surprisingly more accessible because of that.

The "click" I had concerning silent movie is when I started to watch them totally silent. I realized than most of the time, the music written for them afterwards flattened their nuances into one "mood" (IT'S FUNNY LOOK IT'S FUNNY), messed up their inner rhythm, did more bad than good.

It doesn't mean it's necessarily your solution (and today I can enjoy watching some of them with music, specially if it's live at a screening). But it was just my key to watch them differently, to stop searching in them something which was not what they had to offer, but only what I liked in later cinema.

The first step is to stop finding those films excuses: they perfectly know what they wanna do and obtain, they're not clumsy about it, it's just that you're asking them to do something they don't want to. A little like going into a japanese restaurant and waiting for food to taste like pizza.

An exemple would be the litteral and pure emotions, not mixed-up with meta or intellectualism tentative: movies not coming to you with a shield to protect themselves.

Another thing I realized quickly about silent cinema is that I loved the "bubble" side of them. Like a dream, a little like when you hear sound only under water : all is like mental/dreamy and slow, you take all the time you want to contemplate a visage, you're like in another time-space, some images seem like visions. Take some shots of *Nosferatu*: there are not the more clean-up perfect images, but they have something primitive, archaic, which is fascinating. I loved watch them in my bed, in the dark and the silence to watch them (a good bunch of shots of silents cinema is not really a square, but a spot of light, like light appearing in the dark).

Another thing I realized after some time is that their is not "one" silent cinema, but a lot of very different ways to do silent cinema. Between the very first films (a little before 1895) and the very last ones (until 1936 in Japan), there is as much time, narrative and esthetics changes, than between *Breathless* and *Matrix*! When you start, you see all silent cinema like "people doing big gestures silently with inter-titles", but watching it, you realize there is nothing in common, even in the mise en scene itself, between a danish drama of the early 10's, a hollywood cosmic melodrama of the late 20's, a documentary-shot from the UK Norden in th early 1900's, and avant-garde german film of the early 20's... It's a lot of different worlds.

And don't forget to watch those films with the same exigence you would have for others: in their right speed (not speed up, most silent are around 16-18fps), with their colors when they exist (and it's often the case), in a good quality and not in a over-compressed youtube video, etc.

Have a good screening!


PS: [I sum-up some films excerpt for silent films on website](https://www.cinexploria.fr/category/cinema-muet/) i you want to look for things to try, it's in french (but often with titles in english).

There's no requirement to contextualize films in order to enjoy them. If you don't like pre-talkies, that's perfectly fine. You're in the 99%. There are people who insist that you can't enjoy Kurosawa without a degree in Japanese history. That's complete bullshit.

Passion of Joan of Arc was, for me, one of the lamest things I've ever watched. There are thousands of other films out there to enjoy. Don't force yourself to watch movies you don't like.
This. Not sure where you live, but find a historic theater with a Wurlitzer as they periodically have live shows of silent movies.
Yeah, I would have much rather started with the more dramatic silent films.

Start with short subjects: try Keaton - The Goat, One Week, Convict 13; try Chaplin’s The Immigrant. For more serious fare, look at A Corner in Wheat and Musketeers of Pig Alley by Griffith (and approach them in terms of the qualities of the photography).

For longer stuff, try Sunrise. 

Don’t approach them with the sense that they’re going to win you over — start with the assumption that these are all time greats and maybe you have to work to love yourself to their wavelength. It’ll be worth it.

do yourself a favor and watch alexander nevsky, directed my eisenstein, score by prokofiev.  one of my all time favorites.  babies thrown in fires, the battle on the ice is stunning and not just for its time.

There are so many eras of film to explore that it’s not worth trying to force it with something that’s not clicking. If you’re primarily interested in watching older stuff just move into the 30s. Tons of 30s movies that are much more modern in their approach.
Do you think the silent version is better than the talking version of AQotWF?
Came here to say Buster Keaton, yes
I found Buster Keaton very digestible immediately as someone who grew up exposed to Looney Toons.

When talkies came along, the audience no longer felt it was necessary to keep looking at the screen as attentively. So the visual spectacle didn't have to convey as much meaning. Silent films require a bit more imagination, almost like reading a book compared to hearing it. Most silent films are about a century old, so they're going to be harder to relate to culturally and because we're used to modern filmmaking. One thing you could do is learn film theory. Early fillmakers like Eisenstein and Griffith created the grammar of filmmaking. The Story of Film and Martin Scorseses film about American movies would help with appreciating them more.

You should watch Sherlock Jr. It's his masterpiece and a short film. Others would say The General is his greatest film. But that one is much longer, so it wouldn't recommend that first for someone struggling to watch silent films. Another great silent short is the experimental film Meshes of the Afternoon. Maybe Chaplin's The Kid might pull at your heart strings. If you see The Gold Rush I'd see the original version before seeing the shortened narrated version.

I think it might help to try and relax your mind and expectations. I haven’t seen a lot of silent films but I have city lights and had no issue watching it. But I sometimes find older films relaxing anyway. I think it might take you a while and I’d wait for it to really click and not force yourself.

It was kinda hard for me to get into silent films as well. When I started what helped is 20 minutes increments. No matter what silent film unless it was really capturing me I would only watch 20 minutes, think about what I watched, come back at a later time and watch another 20 minutes. Idk if eventually this just created an appreciation for them or what but eventually I wouldn't always have to do that.
I am more favorable to the silent version. But they’re very different movies.

Fritz Lang has some other good ones. Dr. Mabuse The Gambler, and Die Nibelungen parts 1 & 2 are all amazing. You might also like Hitchcock's The Lodger. I also echo The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari. 

If you want to keep trying with Chaplin, my favorite is The Gold Rush.

When I studied in cinema I knew nothing of silent films except for Chaplin. But then we learned about the invention of cinema and seeing those first few short films put into historical context made them worth watching. I mean, they are super boring films like workers coming out of a factory or stuff like that but you get the idea: it was a brand new invention.

After that and only a few years into this new way a telling stories, you get these crazy filmmakers doing really impressive stuff for the first time. That’s how I get to enjoy these silent movies: when they are put into their historical context.
Did you have to buy a physical copy to watch that?
Out of curiosity, how are you watching them?
I strongly suggest you to watch Buster Keaton movies, my pick is "the general". It is a true action movie

I loved *The General* but struggled to connect with any other silent films until I watched *Our Dancing Daughters*, which I was interested in because of its star: a very young Joan Crawford. This became my way into several other silent films, including The Unknown (Crawford), Manhandled (Gloria Swanson), Flesh and the Devil (Greta Garbo), Don Juan (John Barrymore), The Wind (Lillian Gish) and The Last Command (William Powell).

I think it's important to remember that watching films of any kind is 'mood dependant' by that I simply mean, you can only enjoy / appreciate any film if you are in the right mood for it, and vice versa, cannot enjoy any film you are not in the mood for. Therefore, you have to be in a patient mood in order to watch any slow film, not just silent cinema but for instance an Ozu pictures. What often works for me is seeing silent pictures during the evening when I'm slowing down and can handle that slow pace. Many other people will say this already but for the record, a great place to start is always the silent comedies by Chaplin, Keaton and Harold Lloyd (my favourites being : The Circus, The General, City Lights, Modern Times, Girlshy, Safety Last and Seven Chances) but also many of the great dramas such as Metropolis, Napoleon, Die Nibelungen and He who gets slapped. But I also understand that silent pictures are an acquired taste of sorts and not everybody's cup of tea

I just checked and saw I watched it in 2012, so I was still on a Netflix disc plan then. If you’re in the United States it’s currently streaming on Tubi.

I watched Metropolis the "new" restoration from 2010. I was surprised how easy it was to watch. I was so surprised by the resolution it's possible to get from the old film stock. It's also fascinating the movie will be 100 years old in a few years.

You mention city of lights. I haven't watched any comedy silent movies that have slapstick elements from that era either. maybe I will some day, but it's not on top of the list exactly.

As for how to approach old silent film. When I watch really old movies I don't necessarily watch for pure entertainment, but for my overall interest in movies and movie history.

1. Avoid poor releases. Don’t watch trash public domain uploads. Unrestored, inappropriate music wrong speeds etc.

2. As many people have said, I think Buster Keaton works for a lot of modern viewers. His films move fast and his physical skills are timeless

3. If you like Horror, Try Phantom of The Opera or Caligari.

You are 100% right about the releases. I watched a silent on TCM that was just over an hour long but the versions on YouTube ran over a half hour longer.
I consider myself a fan of silent film but for the life of me I don't know what you see in The Fall of the House of Usher. I found it incredibly unimpressive. What am I missing?

The Man Who Laughs has excellent pathos and melodrama (from the main cast, at least). I found the performances to be much fuller and more sincere than a lot of the wildly exaggerated performances that are common in other films of the era.

I know you asked for how, not which films... But try The General (action movie basically, if this doesn't impress you I don't know what to tell you), Sherlock Jr (maybe more dated but likely to impress you/anyone for being innovative and ahead of it's time), or Phantom Carriage

I don’t think setting City Lights as the test for whether someone will like silent films is a very good idea. I like the ending, but wasn’t much of a fan of it, and I like silent films. I liked The General significantly more. 

Really what op needs is the technological, artistic, and cultural context and to try a variety of films. Maybe they’d like Keaton, maybe Chaplin, maybe Griffith, maybe Murnau.
